## Resume tips
Studios spend under a minute on each resume. Here's how to make that minute count.

Most first resumes fail for one reason: they list duties instead of results. A mentor reading fifty applications is looking for proof that you can finish something.

## What mentors told us
We asked mentors across our partner studios what makes them read on. The answers were the same every time: one page, real work, and a link they can click.

- Put your best project at the top, with one line on what you did
- Swap "responsible for" with what changed because of you
- Add one link to a portfolio, GitHub or writing sample

> A short resume with one great project beats a long one with ten small ones.

## Try it this week
Open your resume, cut it to one page and rewrite your top three lines as results. Then apply to one internship today.

## First internship
Every mentor on Primer says the same thing: you're not expected to know everything on day one.

Most interns who struggle don't struggle because the work is hard. They struggle because they wait too long to ask. A good internship makes the next step clear: watch how it's done, then do it.

## What we've seen
Across 3,000+ placements, the interns who get offers do two things. They ask questions early, and they share unfinished work before it's polished.

- Ask one question a day, even a small one
- Share your work at the halfway point, not the end
- Read your mentor's notes before the next review

> The best time to ask for feedback is before you think you're ready.

## Try it this week
Pick one task, set a timer for an hour and get a rough version done. Then show it to your mentor and take it from there.

## Interview prep
What mentors ask in a first interview, and how to walk them through your work in ten minutes.

A portfolio interview isn't a test. It's a conversation about how you think. The mentor wants to know what you made, why you made it that way and what you'd change.

## The questions that come up
- What was the brief, and what did you decide first?
- What went wrong, and what did you do about it?
- What would you do differently with another week?

> Show one project in depth rather than five on the surface.

## Try it this week
Pick your strongest project and practise telling its story out loud in five minutes: the brief, the decision, the result. Then book a mock interview.

## Applying
The two weeks after you apply are the best time to get ready. Here's a simple plan.

Waiting is the hardest part of applying. The students who do best use it: they keep building, so they have something new to talk about in the interview.

## A two-week plan
- Spend twenty minutes a day on one small project related to the role
- Read the company's recent work and note two things you'd ask about
- Do one mock interview with a friend or a mentor

> Keep applying while you wait. One application is a hope; five are a plan.

## When the email comes
Reply within a day, confirm the interview time and send your portfolio link again so it's at the top of their inbox.

## Inside Primer
Paid stipends, a named mentor and real work. Behind the scenes of how a company gets listed on Primer.

Before a single role goes live, we talk to the team that will host the intern. We want to know who the mentor is, what the intern will actually do each week and how much they will be paid.

## What every listing needs
- A monthly stipend, shown on the listing
- A named mentor who reviews work every week
- A plan for each month of the internship

> If a company can't tell us what the intern will do in week one, the role isn't ready.

## After the internship
Every intern rates their placement when it ends. Studios that slip below our bar stop posting until we've talked it through.

## Intern stories
Ananya had never worked in a studio. Four months later she was hanging a museum show.

She found the studio assistant internship on a Sunday night, applied with a link to her college project and a few lines on why. Two weeks later she was on a video call with her future mentor.

## What made the difference
- She sent work she was proud of, not everything she had made
- She asked questions in her first week instead of guessing
- She kept a diary of each Friday review and acted on it

> I stopped trying to look like I knew everything, and started learning.

## What's next
Ananya is now a full-time studio assistant, and she mentors the next intern herself.

## About the role
Work directly inside the studio of fine artist Lena Hart as she prepares a solo museum exhibition. The studio assistant will gain first-hand experience building heavy stretcher bars, preparing mineral pigments, mixing rabbit-skin glue gesso, and managing international gallery freight logistics.

## What you'll work on
- Construct custom heavy-duty mortise stretcher bars up to 3 meters in length.
- Stretch raw Belgian linen taut without warping and apply traditional hot size coatings.
- Mull dry earth and mineral pigments with linseed oil, walnut oil, and damar varnish.
- Pack and crate delicate high-relief textured canvases for shipping to Basel and London galleries.

## What you'll learn
- Month 1: Substrate & Gesso Calibration. Build and prime 12 large-format canvases to precise museum exhibition tension standards.
- Month 2-3: Pigment Formulation & Studio Support. Mull raw lapis, ochre, and slate pigments and assist on high-relief impasto layers.
- Month 4: Museum Crating & Exhibition Install. Construct foam-lined travel crates and assist gallery preparators during museum hanging.

## Eligibility
- Fine arts student or studio practitioner with genuine physical energy and care for materials.
- Experience stretching canvas, using power saws, and handling wet oil mediums.
- Attention to detail, order, and cleanliness in a professional working atelier.
- Enthusiasm for contemporary abstract painting and gallery operations.

## Timeline
Starts May 1, 2027 · apply by April 1, 2027 · 4 Months · Full-time (36 hrs/wk) · 2 openings.
